lead: A transmitter turns digital baseband samples into an RF signal at the antenna with the right power, in the right channel, and without spilling into the neighbouring channels. It mirrors the receiver, but its limits are output power, efficiency and the spectral mask rather than noise. In a transceiver both halves share an antenna and often a synthesizer, so the strong transmit signal must be kept out of the sensitive receiver.
prereq: You need: compression and IM3 and the receiver plans of receiver architectures.

blocks.text: Digital baseband produces two sample streams, I and Q. A digital-to-analog converter (DAC) turns each into a voltage, and a reconstruction low-pass filter removes the DAC's sampling images. The I/Q (quadrature) modulator forms I(t) cos ω<sub>LO</sub>t − Q(t) sin ω<sub>LO</sub>t, which places the complex baseband signal at f<sub>LO</sub> with one sideband only. A driver amplifier lifts the level, the power amplifier (PA) sets the output power, a harmonic low-pass filter removes 2f<sub>LO</sub> and 3f<sub>LO</sub>, and a duplexer or a transmit/receive switch connects the antenna.

Direct up-conversion has two weaknesses: LO feedthrough leaves a spur at f<sub>LO</sub> in mid-channel, and the large PA output at the VCO's own frequency can couple back and pull the VCO (LO pulling). Running the VCO at 2f<sub>LO</sub> and dividing by 2 cures pulling.

Two-step up-conversion first mixes baseband to a fixed IF, filters it, then mixes to RF with a second LO. The second mixer creates f<sub>LO2</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub> and f<sub>LO2</sub> − f<sub>IF</sub>; an RF band-pass filter keeps one and removes the other, called the unwanted sideband. With f<sub>IF</sub> = 400 MHz and f<sub>LO2</sub> = 2.0 GHz, the wanted output is 2.4 GHz and the unwanted sideband 1.6 GHz, far enough apart to filter easily. The cost is a second synthesizer, an IF filter and more power.

sections.h3: Output power, EIRP, ACLR and the spectral mask

blocks.where: EIRP (effective isotropic radiated power) in dBm; P<sub>PA</sub> is the PA output in dBm; L<sub>feed</sub> is the total loss in dB of the harmonic filter, duplexer or switch and cable between the PA and the antenna; G<sub>ant</sub> is the antenna gain in dBi. If the power at the antenna port P<sub>ant</sub> is already known, EIRP = P<sub>ant</sub> + G<sub>ant</sub>, with no loss term.

blocks.text: A spectral mask is a regulatory or standard limit on transmitted power against frequency offset from the carrier, given as absolute power in a measurement bandwidth. The adjacent-channel leakage ratio (ACLR) is the power in the wanted channel divided by the power that leaks into the adjacent channel, in dB; some syllabi call it the adjacent-channel power ratio (ACPR). A larger ACLR is better: 45 dB means the adjacent channel receives 45 dB less power than the wanted one. PA compression and IM3 widen the spectrum (spectral regrowth) and lower ACLR, and I/Q gain and phase error add an image sideband.

Modulated signals have a peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR), so the average output must be backed off from compression by about the PAPR: an 8 dB PAPR signal at 25 dBm average has 33 dBm peaks. The PA is chosen so these peaks stay near or below P1dB,out, or linearised as in RF power amplifiers.

sections.h3: Transceivers: duplexer, TDD switch and shared LO

blocks.text: In frequency-division duplex (FDD) the transmitter and receiver work at the same time on two frequencies, joined to one antenna by a duplexer: two band-pass filters, one for each band. Its insertion loss (typically 1 to 3 dB in a handset) appears twice: it cuts the EIRP on transmit, and on receive it adds directly to the noise figure because it sits before the LNA. Its isolation keeps two things out of the receiver: the transmit carrier itself, which can compress the LNA, and the PA's noise in the receive band, which adds to the receiver's own noise floor.

In time-division duplex (TDD) the two directions take turns on one frequency, so a switch replaces the duplexer. The switch has lower loss but finite isolation, and the PA must be off before the LNA is connected; a guard period covers the switching time. One synthesizer can feed both mixers in TDD; in FDD the transmit and receive LOs differ by the duplex spacing, so two synthesizers or an offset scheme are used. The LO's phase noise matters on both sides: on transmit it spreads into the adjacent channel, and on receive a strong blocker mixes with it (reciprocal mixing).

examples.question: In a direct-conversion transmitter the I/Q modulator gives −5 dBm, the driver has 10 dB gain and the PA 20 dB gain with P1dB,out = 33 dBm. The harmonic filter loses 0.5 dB and the duplexer 1.5 dB; the antenna gain is 3 dBi. The signal has PAPR = 8 dB and the PA achieves ACLR = 45 dB. Find the PA output, the antenna-port power, the EIRP in dBm and watts, the peak power at the PA output and the power leaked into the adjacent channel at the antenna port.
steps: L<sub>feed</sub> = 0.5 + 1.5 = 2 dB, so P<sub>ant</sub> = 25 − 2 = 23 dBm (200 mW).
EIRP = 23 + 3 = 26 dBm = 10<sup>2.6</sup> mW = 398 mW, about 0.40 W. The same from P<sub>PA</sub> − L<sub>feed</sub> + G<sub>ant</sub> = 25 − 2 + 3.
Peak PA output = 25 + 8 = 33 dBm, exactly P1dB,out: the peaks reach 1 dB of compression, so this is the most average power the PA can give without linearisation.
Adjacent-channel power at the antenna port = 23 − 45 = −22 dBm (6.3 µW).
examples.answer: P<sub>PA</sub> = 25 dBm, P<sub>ant</sub> = 23 dBm, EIRP = 26 dBm (0.40 W), peaks at 33 dBm (right at P1dB,out), adjacent-channel leakage −22 dBm.

examples.question: The same 25 dBm PA feeds an FDD duplexer. The duplexer isolates the receiver from the transmit port by 50 dB at the transmit frequency and by 45 dB in the receive band. The PA's output noise in the receive band is −130 dBm/Hz. The receiver has NF = 3 dB and its LNA has P1dB,in = −15 dBm. Find the transmit carrier at the LNA input, the transmit noise at the LNA input, and the desensitisation. What receive-band isolation keeps the desensitisation below 0.2 dB?
steps: Carrier at the LNA: 25 − 50 = −25 dBm, 10 dB below the LNA's P1dB,in of −15 dBm: no compression, but the LNA and mixer must still handle it linearly.
Transmit noise at the LNA: −130 − 45 = −175 dBm/Hz.
Receiver's own input noise density: −174 + 3 = −171 dBm/Hz.
Total: 10 log₁₀(10<sup>−17.1</sup> + 10<sup>−17.5</sup>) = −169.5 dBm/Hz, so the noise floor rises by 1.46 dB: the receiver loses 1.46 dB of sensitivity.
With 55 dB isolation the transmit noise is −185 dBm/Hz and the total is −170.8 dBm/Hz: a 0.17 dB rise, below 0.2 dB.
examples.answer: −25 dBm of carrier and −175 dBm/Hz of noise reach the LNA, desensitising it by 1.46 dB; about 55 dB of receive-band isolation (0.17 dB) is needed.

traps: Multiplying dBm by dB. Gains in dB add to powers in dBm: −5 dBm + 30 dB = 25 dBm. Only in milliwatts do you multiply (0.316 mW × 1000 = 316 mW).
Subtracting the feed loss from a power already measured at the antenna port. Count L<sub>feed</sub> once, between the PA and the antenna.
Calling ACLR a mask. ACLR is a ratio in dB relative to the wanted channel; a spectral mask is an absolute limit at each frequency offset.
Setting the average output at P1dB,out. A signal with 8 dB PAPR must average about 8 dB below it, or its peaks clip.
Forgetting that duplexer loss counts on receive too: 1.5 dB of duplexer loss adds 1.5 dB to the receiver noise figure.

quiz.q: Write the EIRP formula and say what each term is.
quiz.a: EIRP = P<sub>PA</sub> − L<sub>feed</sub> + G<sub>ant</sub>: PA output in dBm, loss between PA and antenna in dB, antenna gain in dBi. From the antenna port: EIRP = P<sub>ant</sub> + G<sub>ant</sub>.

quiz.q: A PA gives 20 dBm, the filter loses 1.5 dB and the antenna gain is 2 dBi. Find the EIRP in dBm and mW.
Baseband is up-converted to a 400 MHz IF and then mixed with a 2.0 GHz LO. Give the two RF outputs and say which filter removes the unwanted one.
quiz.a: 2.0 + 0.4 = 2.4 GHz and 2.0 − 0.4 = 1.6 GHz. An RF band-pass filter after the second mixer passes 2.4 GHz and removes the 1.6 GHz sideband.

quiz.q: Define ACLR and give its unit.
quiz.a: The wanted-channel power divided by the power leaked into the adjacent channel, in dB (often written dBc). Larger is better.

quiz.q: Why does duplexer loss lower receiver sensitivity?
quiz.a: It is a passive loss in front of the LNA, so its loss in dB adds straight onto the receiver noise figure, and the sensitivity rises by the same amount.

quiz.q: A transmitter meets its EIRP but fails its spectral mask. Give two likely causes and a fix for each.
quiz.a: PA compression on signal peaks (spectral regrowth): back off further or add digital predistortion. I/Q gain or phase mismatch, or LO phase noise: trim the I/Q paths, or use a cleaner synthesizer.

quiz.q: A TDD radio's transmit/receive switch has poor isolation. What happens to the receiver?
quiz.a: If the PA is still on while the LNA is connected, the transmit power leaks into the LNA and can compress or even damage it; the guard period and switch isolation must stop this.

beyond: Not for the exam. Phones with carrier aggregation carry banks of SAW and BAW duplexers and switches. Full-duplex research cancels the transmitter's leakage in the receiver so both share one frequency. Massive-MIMO base stations put a small transmitter behind each antenna element. Search for 'self-interference cancellation' and 'carrier aggregation front end'.

figure.caption: The worked examples' transmitter: DACs and reconstruction filters feed the I/Q modulator, then the driver, PA, harmonic filter and duplexer take −5 dBm to 23 dBm at the antenna port and 26 dBm EIRP. The duplexer also lets −25 dBm of carrier and −175 dBm/Hz of transmit noise reach the receiver.

spec.aria: Block diagram of a direct-conversion transmitter. I and Q DACs each feed a low-pass filter, both feed an I/Q modulator driven by an LO with 90 degree phase split, giving minus 5 dBm. A driver of plus 10 dB gives 5 dBm, the PA of plus 20 dB gives 25 dBm, the harmonic filter with 0.5 dB loss gives 24.5 dBm and the duplexer with 1.5 dB loss gives 23 dBm at a 3 dBi antenna, for an EIRP of 26 dBm. A branch from the duplexer to the LNA notes minus 25 dBm of carrier and minus 175 dBm per hertz of transmit noise.
